notes.front: What is the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA)?
notes.back: The 1970 federal law requiring consumer reporting agencies to use fair procedures that respect the confidentiality, accuracy, relevance and proper use of consumer information.
notes.explanation: Its effective-date note records enactment on 26 October 1970; the purpose clause ties credit reporting to fairness for the consumer.
notes.example: Like referee rules for the credit scoreboard, setting who may see the scores and how errors are fixed.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681(b)
notes.evidence: It is the purpose of this subchapter to require that consumer reporting agencies adopt reasonable procedures for meeting the needs of commerce for consumer credit, personnel, insurance, and other information in a manner which is fair and equitable to the consumer

notes.front: Under the FCRA, what is a consumer reporting agency (CRA)?
notes.back: Any person that, for fees or on a cooperative non-profit basis, regularly assembles or evaluates consumer information to furnish consumer reports to third parties.
notes.explanation: The definition also requires use of interstate commerce to prepare or furnish the reports.
notes.example: Like a credit bureau that compiles files on people and sells reports to lenders.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(f)
notes.evidence: regularly engages in whole or in part in the practice of assembling or evaluating consumer credit information or other information on consumers for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties

notes.front: Under the FCRA, what is a consumer report?
notes.back: An agency's communication on a consumer's creditworthiness, character or way of life, used to judge eligibility for credit, insurance, employment or other listed purposes.
notes.explanation: The definition turns on who communicates the information and what it is used for.
notes.example: Like a reference letter about your finances and reputation, but written by a bureau and read by a lender or employer.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(d)(1)
notes.evidence: any written, oral, or other communication of any information by a consumer reporting agency bearing on a consumer's credit worthiness, credit standing, credit capacity, character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living

notes.front: What is an investigative consumer report?
notes.back: A consumer report in which information on the consumer's character, reputation or way of life comes from personal interviews with neighbours, friends, associates or others.
notes.explanation: Personal interviews are what set it apart from an ordinary consumer report.
notes.example: Like a background check where an investigator phones your neighbours, rather than just pulling your credit file.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(e)
notes.evidence: information on a consumer's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living is obtained through personal interviews with neighbors, friends, or associates of the consumer

notes.front: What is a permissible purpose under the FCRA?
notes.back: One of the listed circumstances in which a consumer reporting agency may furnish a consumer report; it may furnish reports in no other case.
notes.explanation: The list is closed, so a report furnished outside it breaks the Act.
notes.example: Like a guest list at a door: only people with a listed reason get in.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)
notes.evidence: any consumer reporting agency may furnish a consumer report under the following circumstances and no other

notes.front: Under the FCRA, what is an adverse action?
notes.back: An unfavourable decision such as a denial of credit, insurance or employment, or a worse change in terms.
notes.explanation: For employment, it covers any employment decision that adversely affects a current or prospective employee.
notes.example: Like a lender saying no, or a job offer being withdrawn after a background check.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(k)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: a denial of employment or any other decision for employment purposes that adversely affects any current or prospective employee

notes.front: What is the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act (FACTA)?
notes.back: The 2003 law that amended the FCRA; for example, it set up the centralised source consumers use to request free annual file disclosures.
notes.explanation: The Code notes identify FACTA as Public Law 108-159, enacted on 4 December 2003.
notes.example: Like a 2003 upgrade kit bolted onto a 1970 machine.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681j(a)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: made using the centralized source established for such purpose in accordance with section 211(c) 1 of the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act of 2003
introduces: Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act
uses: Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act

notes.front: What is a fraud alert under the FCRA?
notes.back: A notice a nationwide consumer reporting agency places in a consumer's file, at their request, when they suspect fraud or identity theft.
notes.explanation: The agency must also pass the alert to the other nationwide agencies.
notes.example: Like a "call me first" note on your file that lenders see before opening credit.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c-1(a)(1)
notes.evidence: who asserts in good faith a suspicion that the consumer has been or is about to become a victim of fraud or related crime, including identity theft

notes.front: What is the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA)?
notes.back: A 1999 federal law whose privacy title gives financial institutions a continuing duty to respect customers' privacy and protect their nonpublic personal information.
notes.explanation: The privacy title comes from Public Law 106-102 of 12 November 1999.
notes.example: Like a confidentiality clause written into law for every bank, lender and insurer.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6801(a)
notes.evidence: each financial institution has an affirmative and continuing obligation to respect the privacy of its customers and to protect the security and confidentiality of those customers' nonpublic personal information

notes.front: Under the GLBA, what is a financial institution?
notes.back: Any institution whose business is engaging in financial activities as described in the Bank Holding Company Act, section 1843(k) of title 12.
notes.explanation: The test is the activity, so non-banks such as lenders can be financial institutions.
notes.example: Like classifying a business by what it does, not by its name: a payday lender counts as much as a bank.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6809(3)(A)
notes.evidence: The term "financial institution" means any institution the business of which is engaging in financial activities as described in section 1843(k) of title 12.

notes.front: What is nonpublic personal information (NPI) under the GLBA?
notes.back: Personally identifiable financial information provided by a consumer, resulting from a transaction or service, or otherwise obtained by a financial institution.
notes.explanation: Publicly available information is excluded, as the regulations define it.
notes.example: Like the contents of your bank statement, as opposed to your name in the phone book.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6809(4)(A)
notes.evidence: means personally identifiable financial information- (i) provided by a consumer to a financial institution; (ii) resulting from any transaction with the consumer or any service performed for the consumer; or (iii) otherwise obtained by the financial institution

notes.front: What is pretexting under the GLBA?
notes.back: Obtaining, or trying to obtain, a financial institution's customer information about another person by false statements or forged documents.
notes.explanation: The statute heads the ban "obtaining customer information by false pretenses".
notes.example: Like phoning a bank pretending to be the account holder to learn their balance.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6821(a)
notes.evidence: for any person to obtain or attempt to obtain, or cause to be disclosed or attempt to cause to be disclosed to any person, customer information of a financial institution relating to another person- (1) by making a false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement

notes.front: What is the FTC Safeguards Rule?
notes.back: The FTC rule under the GLBA setting standards for administrative, technical and physical safeguards that protect customer information.
notes.explanation: It covers financial institutions under FTC jurisdiction and implements sections 501 and 505(b)(2) of the GLBA.
notes.example: Like a building security code, but for the customer data of non-bank financial firms.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.1(a), p. 1
notes.evidence: sets forth standards for developing, implementing, and maintaining reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information

notes.front: Under the Safeguards Rule, who is the qualified individual?
notes.back: The person designated to oversee, implement and enforce the information security programme.
notes.explanation: The person may be employed by the institution, an affiliate or a service provider.
notes.example: Like a club's named safety officer, who may be a member or an outside contractor.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(a), p. 7
notes.evidence: Designate a qualified individual responsible for overseeing and implementing your information security program and enforcing your information security program

notes.front: What is the Red Flags Rule?
notes.back: The FTC rule requiring financial institutions and creditors with covered accounts to run a written programme to detect, prevent and mitigate identity theft.
notes.explanation: It applies to those subject to FTC enforcement of the FCRA.
notes.example: Like a shop training cashiers to spot forged notes, but for identity thieves opening accounts.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(1), p. 1
notes.evidence: must develop and implement a written Identity Theft Prevention Program (Program) that is designed to detect, prevent, and mitigate identity theft in connection with the opening of a covered account or any existing covered account

notes.front: Under the Red Flags Rule, what is a covered account?
notes.back: A consumer account permitting multiple payments or transactions, or any other account with a reasonably foreseeable risk of identity theft.
notes.explanation: The Rule gives examples such as credit card, mortgage, car loan, mobile phone, utility, checking and savings accounts.
notes.example: Like any account a thief could open or take over in your name and keep using.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(b)(3), p. 1
notes.evidence: primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, that involves or is designed to permit multiple payments or transactions, such as a credit card account, mortgage loan, automobile loan

notes.front: What is the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Dodd-Frank)?
notes.back: The 2010 federal law (Public Law 111-203) whose title X, the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, set up the consumer financial protection bureau.
notes.explanation: Regulation P cites the Consumer Financial Protection Act as title X of Dodd-Frank; the Bureau section dates from 21 July 2010.
notes.example: Like a major rebuild of the financial rulebook after the 2008 crisis, including a new consumer regulator.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1016 (Regulation P), 2026 edition, § 1016.1(b)(3), p. 2
notes.evidence: Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, title X of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (Dodd-Frank Act), Public Law 111-203
introduces: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act
uses: Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act

notes.front: What is the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)?
notes.back: An independent bureau in the Federal Reserve System that regulates the offering and provision of consumer financial products and services.
notes.explanation: The statute names it the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection; it regulates under the federal consumer financial laws.
notes.example: Like a consumer watchdog dedicated to loans, cards and bank accounts.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5491 (Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection), § 5491(a)
notes.evidence: There is established in the Federal Reserve System, an independent bureau to be known as the "Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection", which shall regulate the offering and provision of consumer financial products or services

notes.front: What are unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices (UDAAP)?
notes.back: Conduct in consumer financial transactions that the CFPB may act to prevent covered persons and service providers from engaging in.
notes.explanation: The CFPB may also make rules identifying such acts or practices as unlawful.
notes.example: Like the FTC's unfair-or-deceptive test, with a third category, "abusive", added for finance.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(a)
notes.evidence: to prevent a covered person or service provider from committing or engaging in an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice under Federal law in connection with any transaction with a consumer for a consumer financial product or service
introduces: unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices
uses: unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices
unfair or deceptive acts or practices

notes.front: What is the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA)?
notes.back: A 1974 federal law protecting the privacy of parents and students in education records at institutions receiving Department of Education funds.
notes.explanation: The FERPA regulations state this purpose; the statutory section was added by Public Law 93-380 on 21 August 1974.
notes.example: Like HIPAA's rules for medical files, but for a school's student files.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.2, p. 2
notes.evidence: The purpose of this part is to set out requirements for the protection of privacy of parents and students under section 444 of the General Education Provisions Act, as amended.
introduces: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
uses: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act

notes.front: Under FERPA, what are education records?
notes.back: Records directly related to a student and maintained by an educational agency or institution, or by a party acting for it.
notes.explanation: The definition then lists exclusions, such as a teacher's private memory aids.
notes.example: Like everything in a student's school file, from grades to disciplinary notes.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Education records", p. 4
notes.evidence: The term means those records that are: (1) Directly related to a student; and (2) Maintained by an educational agency or institution or by a party acting for the agency or institution.

notes.front: Under FERPA, who is an eligible student?
notes.back: A student who has reached 18 or is attending a postsecondary institution.
notes.explanation: Either condition is enough on its own.
notes.example: Like a 17-year-old at university, or an 18-year-old still at secondary school.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Eligible student", p. 5
notes.evidence: Eligible student means a student who has reached 18 years of age or is attending an institution of postsecondary education.

notes.front: Under FERPA, what is directory information?
notes.back: Information in an education record that would not generally be considered harmful or an invasion of privacy if disclosed, such as name and address.
notes.explanation: The list is open: it includes, but is not limited to, the items the regulation names.
notes.example: Like the details printed in a sports programme: name, team, height and weight.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Directory information", p. 3
notes.evidence: Directory information means information contained in an education record of a student that would not generally be considered harmful or an invasion of privacy if disclosed.

notes.front: What is the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA)?
notes.back: A federal law giving parents rights over surveys, analyses and evaluations of students in federally funded programmes, including inspecting the materials used.
notes.explanation: Its section is headed "Protection of pupil rights" at 20 U.S.C. 1232h.
notes.example: Like a parental veto over a school questionnaire on sensitive family matters.
notes.source: 20 U.S.C. § 1232h (protection of pupil rights), § 1232h(a)
notes.evidence: All instructional materials, including teacher's manuals, films, tapes, or other supplementary material which will be used in connection with any survey, analysis, or evaluation as part of any applicable program shall be available for inspection by the parents

notes.front: Which agency generally enforces the FCRA, and under which Act?
notes.back: The FTC, under the FTC Act, except where enforcement is committed to another agency.
notes.explanation: The FTC's authority is also subject to the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681s(a)(1)
notes.evidence: The Federal Trade Commission shall be authorized to enforce compliance with the requirements imposed by this subchapter under the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.), with respect to consumer reporting agencies and all other persons subject thereto

notes.front: Which agency prescribes most regulations under the FCRA?
notes.back: The CFPB, except for the Red Flags provisions in section 1681m(e) and the disposal provision in section 1681w.
notes.explanation: The statute gives the rulemaking power to "the Bureau", with those two carve-outs.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681s(e)(1)
notes.evidence: The Bureau shall prescribe such regulations as are necessary to carry out the purposes of this subchapter, except with respect to sections 1681m(e) and 1681w of this title.

notes.front: A consumer group wants a new regulation on how consumer reporting agencies handle disputes. Which agency should it petition?
notes.back: B: the CFPB.
notes.choices:
A) The FTC
B) The CFPB
C) The Department of Education
D) Each state attorney general
notes.choicesExplained: A: the FTC enforces the FCRA but most rulemaking sits with the Bureau. C: education is unrelated. D: states enforce but do not write FCRA regulations.
notes.explanation: The FCRA gives the Bureau the power to prescribe the regulations needed to carry out the Act, outside two carve-outs.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681s(e)(1)
notes.evidence: The Bureau shall prescribe such regulations as are necessary to carry out the purposes of this subchapter

notes.front: A firm charges landlords a fee for reports it compiles on tenants' payment histories and court records. How does the FCRA classify the firm?
notes.back: C: a consumer reporting agency.
notes.choices:
A) A furnisher only
B) A financial institution
C) A consumer reporting agency
D) Outside the FCRA, as it is not a bank
notes.choicesExplained: A: furnishers supply information to agencies; this firm assembles and sells reports. B: that is a GLBA term. D: being a bank is not part of the definition.
notes.explanation: Regularly assembling consumer information for a fee to furnish reports to third parties fits the definition.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(f)
notes.evidence: which, for monetary fees, dues, or on a cooperative nonprofit basis, regularly engages in whole or in part in the practice of assembling or evaluating consumer credit information or other information on consumers

notes.front: What are three eligibility decisions for which a communication can be a consumer report?
notes.back: Personal, family or household credit or insurance; employment; and any other purpose authorised under section 1681b.
notes.explanation: Use, or expected use, for one of these purposes is part of the definition.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(d)(1)
notes.evidence: for the purpose of serving as a factor in establishing the consumer's eligibility for- (A) credit or insurance to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes; (B) employment purposes; or (C) any other purpose authorized under section 1681b

notes.front: Which permissible purpose lets a consumer reporting agency answer a federal grand jury?
notes.back: A court order, or a subpoena issued in connection with federal grand jury proceedings.
notes.explanation: It is the first permissible purpose listed.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)(1)
notes.evidence: In response to the order of a court having jurisdiction to issue such an order, a subpoena issued in connection with proceedings before a Federal grand jury

notes.front: Which permissible purpose depends entirely on the consumer's own wishes?
notes.back: The written instructions of the consumer to whom the report relates.
notes.explanation: It is the second permissible purpose listed.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)(2)
notes.evidence: In accordance with the written instructions of the consumer to whom it relates.

notes.front: Which permissible purpose covers screening job applicants?
notes.back: Use of the information for employment purposes.
notes.explanation: Other FCRA conditions apply to employment reports, covered with workplace privacy.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)(3)(B)
notes.evidence: intends to use the information for employment purposes

notes.front: Which permissible purpose covers a legitimate business need?
notes.back: A business transaction initiated by the consumer, or reviewing an account to see if the consumer still meets its terms.
notes.explanation: The need must be tied to a consumer-initiated transaction or an existing account.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)(3)(F)
notes.evidence: otherwise has a legitimate business need for the information- (i) in connection with a business transaction that is initiated by the consumer; or (ii) to review an account to determine whether the consumer continues to meet the terms of the account

notes.front: A car dealer's employee pulls the credit report of a celebrity who has never visited the dealership, out of curiosity. Is there a permissible purpose?
notes.back: D: no, curiosity is not a listed purpose.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, a legitimate business need
B) Yes, because dealers extend credit
C) Yes, if the report is not shared
D) No, curiosity is not a listed purpose
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the business-need and credit purposes require a transaction involving the consumer. C: confidentiality afterwards does not create a purpose.
notes.explanation: Agencies may furnish reports only in the listed circumstances "and no other".
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(a)
notes.evidence: any consumer reporting agency may furnish a consumer report under the following circumstances and no other

notes.front: For a transaction the consumer did not initiate, when may an agency furnish consumer report information for prescreened offers?
notes.back: When the transaction is a firm offer of credit or insurance, and the consumer has not elected to be excluded.
notes.explanation: The agency must also operate the opt-out system the statute requires.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681b(c)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: the transaction consists of a firm offer of credit or insurance

notes.front: After an adverse action based on a consumer report, what must the user tell the consumer about the agency?
notes.back: Its name, address and telephone number, and that it did not make the decision and cannot give the reasons.
notes.explanation: Nationwide agencies must include a toll-free number.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681m(a)(3)
notes.evidence: a statement that the consumer reporting agency did not make the decision to take the adverse action and is unable to provide the consumer the specific reasons why the adverse action was taken

notes.front: Which two consumer rights must an adverse action notice mention?
notes.back: A free copy of the report from the agency within 60 days, and the right to dispute its accuracy or completeness.
notes.explanation: The notice must indicate the 60-day window for the free copy.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681m(a)(4)
notes.evidence: a free copy of a consumer report on the consumer from the consumer reporting agency referred to in paragraph (3), which notice shall include an indication of the 60-day period under that section for obtaining such a copy; and (B) to dispute

notes.front: An insurer raises a customer's premium because of items in her consumer report. What must the insurer do?
notes.back: A: give her an adverse action notice, including the agency's details and her rights.
notes.choices:
A) Give her an adverse action notice, including the agency's details and her rights
B) Nothing, as she was not refused cover
C) Ask the agency to notify her
D) Delete the report
notes.choicesExplained: B: an increase in any charge for insurance is an adverse action. C: the duty falls on the user who takes the action. D: deleting the report is not required.
notes.explanation: Increasing a charge for insurance is an adverse action, triggering the user's notice duties.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681a(k)(1)(B)(i)
notes.evidence: a denial or cancellation of, an increase in any charge for, or a reduction or other adverse or unfavorable change in the terms of coverage or amount of, any insurance

notes.front: Most adverse information (other than criminal convictions) may not appear in a consumer report once it is more than {{c1::seven}} years old.
notes.back: seven
notes.explanation: Paid tax liens and accounts placed for collection follow the same seven-year limit.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(a)(5)
notes.evidence: Any other adverse item of information, other than records of convictions of crimes which antedates the report by more than seven years.

notes.front: How long may civil suits, judgments and arrest records stay in a consumer report?
notes.back: Seven years from entry, or until the statute of limitations expires, whichever is longer.
notes.explanation: The longer-of rule means seven years is a minimum, not always the limit.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(a)(2)
notes.evidence: Civil suits, civil judgments, and records of arrest that, from date of entry, antedate the report by more than seven years or until the governing statute of limitations has expired, whichever is the longer period.

notes.front: Bankruptcy cases may be reported until they are more than {{c1::10}} years old.
notes.explanation: The period runs from the order for relief or the date of adjudication.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(a)(1)
notes.evidence: Cases under title 11 or under the Bankruptcy Act that, from the date of entry of the order for relief or the date of adjudication, as the case may be, antedate the report by more than 10 years.

notes.front: When do the FCRA time limits on old adverse information not apply?
notes.back: For credit or life insurance of $150,000 or more, or employment at a salary of $75,000 or more.
notes.explanation: These are the dollar thresholds written in the statute.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(b)
notes.evidence: a principal amount of $150,000 or more; (2) the underwriting of life insurance involving, or which may reasonably be expected to involve, a face amount of $150,000 or more; or (3) the employment of any individual at an annual salary which equals, or which may reasonably be expected to equal $75,000, or more

notes.front: A consumer report for a $20,000 car loan lists an account sent to collection nine years ago. Is that allowed?
notes.back: C: no, collection accounts older than seven years must be left out.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, collection accounts stay for ten years
B) Yes, because it is a car loan
C) No, collection accounts older than seven years must be left out
D) Only if the consumer agrees
notes.choicesExplained: A: ten years applies to bankruptcy cases. B: the loan is below the $150,000 exemption. D: consent is not an exception.
notes.explanation: Accounts placed for collection may not be reported once more than seven years old, and this loan is below the exemption threshold.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(a)(4)
notes.evidence: Accounts placed for collection or charged to profit and loss which antedate the report by more than seven years.

notes.front: When a consumer disputes an item in their file, how long does the agency have to reinvestigate, and at what cost?
notes.back: 30 days from receiving the notice, free of charge.
notes.explanation: The agency must record the current status or delete the item within that period.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681i(a)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: the agency shall, free of charge, conduct a reasonable reinvestigation to determine whether the disputed information is inaccurate and record the current status of the disputed information, or delete the item from the file in accordance with paragraph (5), before the end of the 30-day period

notes.front: When can the 30-day reinvestigation period be extended, and by how much?
notes.back: By up to 15 days, if the consumer sends relevant information during the 30 days.
notes.explanation: The statute limits when this extension may be used.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681i(a)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: may be extended for not more than 15 additional days if the consumer reporting agency receives information from the consumer during that 30-day period that is relevant to the reinvestigation

notes.front: What must an agency do with a disputed item that turns out inaccurate, incomplete or unverifiable?
notes.back: Promptly delete or modify it, and promptly notify the furnisher.
notes.explanation: An item that cannot be verified is treated the same way as an inaccurate one.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681i(a)(5)(A)
notes.evidence: is found to be inaccurate or incomplete or cannot be verified, the consumer reporting agency shall- (i) promptly delete that item of information from the file of the consumer, or modify that item

notes.front: A consumer disputes a debt in her file. After 30 days the agency cannot get the creditor to confirm it. What must the agency do?
notes.back: B: delete or modify the item and notify the furnisher.
notes.choices:
A) Keep it, as silence is not proof of error
B) Delete or modify the item and notify the furnisher
C) Charge her for a longer investigation
D) Keep it but add a note
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: unverifiable items must be deleted or modified. C: reinvestigation is free of charge.
notes.explanation: Information that cannot be verified must be promptly deleted or modified.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681i(a)(5)(A)
notes.evidence: an item of the information is found to be inaccurate or incomplete or cannot be verified, the consumer reporting agency shall- (i) promptly delete

notes.front: What may a furnisher not send to a consumer reporting agency?
notes.back: Information about a consumer that it knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, is inaccurate.
notes.explanation: This is the first of the furnisher accuracy duties.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681s-2(a)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: A person shall not furnish any information relating to a consumer to any consumer reporting agency if the person knows or has reasonable cause to believe that the information is inaccurate.

notes.front: What may an electronically printed card receipt show under FACTA's truncation rule?
notes.back: No more than the last 5 digits of the card number, and not the expiration date.
notes.explanation: The rule applies only to electronically printed receipts, not handwritten or imprinted ones.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c(g)(1)
notes.evidence: shall print more than the last 5 digits of the card number or the expiration date upon any receipt provided to the cardholder at the point of the sale or transaction

notes.front: How often must the nationwide consumer reporting agencies give a consumer their file disclosure free of charge on request?
notes.back: Once during any 12-month period.
notes.explanation: For the nationwide agencies, the request must go through the centralised source set up under FACTA.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681j(a)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: shall make all disclosures pursuant to section 1681g of this title once during any 12-month period upon request of the consumer and without charge to the consumer

notes.front: How long does an initial fraud alert last?
notes.back: At least one year from the request, unless the consumer asks to remove it sooner.
notes.explanation: The consumer only needs a good-faith suspicion of fraud or identity theft.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c-1(a)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: include a fraud alert in the file of that consumer, and also provide that alert along with any credit score generated in using that file, for a period of not less than 1 year

notes.front: What must a consumer submit for an extended fraud alert, and how long does it last?
notes.back: An identity theft report; the alert lasts seven years.
notes.explanation: The agency also excludes the consumer from prescreened lists for five years.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c-1(b)(1)
notes.evidence: who submits an identity theft report to a consumer reporting agency described in section 1681a(p) of this title that maintains a file on the consumer

notes.front: What does an initial fraud alert tell prospective users of the consumer's report?
notes.back: That the consumer does not authorise new credit, extra cards or credit-limit increases in their name without the steps the Act requires.
notes.explanation: The notice is built into each initial and active duty alert.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c-1(h)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: the consumer does not authorize the establishment of any new credit plan or extension of credit, other than under an open-end credit plan

notes.front: A man finds a credit card opened in his name, files an identity theft report and gives it to a nationwide agency. Which alert fits, and for how long?
notes.back: D: an extended fraud alert, for seven years.
notes.choices:
A) An initial alert, for 90 days
B) An active duty alert, for 12 months
C) An initial alert, for one year
D) An extended fraud alert, for seven years
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Act sets at least one year for initial alerts. B: active duty alerts are for military consumers. C: an initial alert needs only suspicion; his identity theft report qualifies him for the extended alert.
notes.explanation: Submitting an identity theft report supports an extended alert lasting seven years.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681c-1(b)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: during the 7-year period beginning on the date of such request

notes.front: Before using consumer information from an affiliate to send marketing solicitations, what must a company give the consumer?
notes.back: Clear notice that the information may be shared for that purpose, and a simple way to opt out.
notes.explanation: An opt-out lasts at least five years.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 41, subchapter III (Fair Credit Reporting Act), § 1681s-3(a)(1)
notes.evidence: the consumer is provided an opportunity and a simple method to prohibit the making of such solicitations to the consumer by such person

notes.front: An online company offers short-term personal loans; it has no bank charter. Is it a GLBA financial institution?
notes.back: A: yes, lending is a financial activity.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, lending is a financial activity
B) No, only chartered banks are covered
C) No, online firms are exempt
D) Only if it takes deposits
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: the definition turns on financial activities, not charters or deposits. C: the Act has no online exemption.
notes.explanation: An institution is covered if its business is engaging in financial activities, whatever its charter.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6809(3)(A)
notes.evidence: any institution the business of which is engaging in financial activities

notes.front: Is publicly available information nonpublic personal information?
notes.back: No, but a list of consumers derived using nonpublic personal information is included.
notes.explanation: A customer list built from account data can therefore be nonpublic personal information even if names are public.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6809(4)(B)–(C)
notes.evidence: Such term does not include publicly available information, as such term is defined by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title.

notes.front: A bank compiles a list of customers with balances over $100,000 to sell to a boat dealer. Is the list nonpublic personal information?
notes.back: C: yes, it is a grouping of consumers derived using nonpublic personal information.
notes.choices:
A) No, names are public
B) No, balances are not personal
C) Yes, it is a grouping of consumers derived using nonpublic personal information
D) Only if account numbers are included
notes.choicesExplained: A: a list derived from nonpublic data is included even if names are public. B: balances result from transactions with the consumer. D: account numbers are not needed.
notes.explanation: Any list or grouping of consumers derived using nonpublic personal information is within the term.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6809(4)(C)(i)
notes.evidence: shall include any list, description, or other grouping of consumers (and publicly available information pertaining to them) that is derived using any nonpublic personal information

notes.front: Under Regulation P, how does a customer differ from a consumer?
notes.back: A customer is a consumer with a customer relationship: a continuing relationship in which the institution provides financial products or services.
notes.explanation: The GLBA ties its privacy notices to establishing and continuing a customer relationship.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1016 (Regulation P), 2026 edition, § 1016.3(i)–(j), p. 4
notes.evidence: Customer means a consumer who has a customer relationship with you. (j)(1) Customer relationship means a continuing relationship between a consumer and you

notes.front: When must a financial institution give customers its GLBA privacy notice?
notes.back: When the customer relationship is established, and at least annually while it continues.
notes.explanation: The notice must describe policies on disclosing nonpublic personal information to affiliates and non-affiliated third parties.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6803(a)
notes.evidence: At the time of establishing a customer relationship with a consumer and not less than annually during the continuation of such relationship, a financial institution shall provide a clear and conspicuous disclosure

notes.front: A credit union opens a savings account for a new member in January and changed its sharing policy in June. When does the member get privacy notices?
notes.back: B: at account opening, and at least annually while the relationship continues.
notes.choices:
A) Only when she asks
B) At account opening, and at least annually while the relationship continues
C) Only once, at account opening
D) Only when the account closes
notes.choicesExplained: A: the notice is required without a request. C: the annual notice exception is lost when policies change. D: the Act ties notices to the start and continuation of the relationship.
notes.explanation: Notices are due when the customer relationship is established and not less than annually.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6803(a)
notes.evidence: At the time of establishing a customer relationship with a consumer and not less than annually during the continuation of such relationship

notes.front: Before disclosing nonpublic personal information to a non-affiliated third party, what must a financial institution give the consumer?
notes.back: Clear notice of the possible disclosure, a chance to opt out before it first happens, and an explanation of how to opt out.
notes.explanation: The opt-out must be available before the information is initially disclosed.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(b)(1)
notes.evidence: the consumer is given the opportunity, before the time that such information is initially disclosed, to direct that such information not be disclosed to such third party; and (C) the consumer is given an explanation of how the consumer can exercise that nondisclosure option

notes.front: Does the GLBA opt-out apply when a bank gives customer data to a firm that markets the bank's own products for it?
notes.back: No: disclosures to third parties performing services for the institution, including marketing its own products, are excepted.
notes.explanation: The exception also covers joint marketing agreements between financial institutions that meet the regulations.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(b)(2)
notes.evidence: providing nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party to perform services for or functions on behalf of the financial institution, including marketing of the financial institution's own products or services

notes.front: What may a financial institution never give a non-affiliated third party for telemarketing, direct mail or email marketing?
notes.back: A consumer's account number or similar access number or code for a credit card, deposit or transaction account.
notes.explanation: Disclosure to a consumer reporting agency is not caught by this limit.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(d)
notes.evidence: an account number or similar form of access number or access code for a credit card account, deposit account, or transaction account of a consumer to any nonaffiliated third party for use in telemarketing, direct mail marketing

notes.front: A mortgage lender wants to sell customer names and loan balances to an unrelated home-insurance agency for its own marketing. What does the GLBA require first?
notes.back: D: a privacy notice and a chance for each customer to opt out before the first disclosure.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as insurers are financial institutions
B) Written opt-in consent from each customer
C) Approval from the CFPB
D) A privacy notice and a chance for each customer to opt out before the first disclosure
notes.choicesExplained: A: the agency is a non-affiliated third party, so the opt-out applies. B: the GLBA uses an opt-out, not opt-in. C: no agency approval is required.
notes.explanation: Disclosure to a non-affiliated third party for its own purposes requires notice and an opportunity to opt out beforehand.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(b)(1)
notes.evidence: A financial institution may not disclose nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party unless

notes.front: Which GLBA exception depends on the consumer's own wishes?
notes.back: Disclosure with the consent or at the direction of the consumer.
notes.explanation: The general exceptions set aside both the notice and the opt-out requirements.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(e)(2)
notes.evidence: with the consent or at the direction of the consumer

notes.front: In a sale or merger of a business unit, may a financial institution disclose that unit's customer information without offering an opt-out?
notes.back: Yes, if the information concerns solely consumers of the business or unit being sold, merged or transferred.
notes.explanation: The GLBA lists proposed or actual sales, mergers, transfers and exchanges among its general exceptions.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6802(e)(7)
notes.evidence: in connection with a proposed or actual sale, merger, transfer, or exchange of all or a portion of a business or operating unit if the disclosure of nonpublic personal information concerns solely consumers of such business or unit

notes.front: When is a state financial privacy law "not inconsistent" with the GLBA?
notes.back: When it gives any person greater protection than the GLBA, as determined by the CFPB after consultation.
notes.explanation: The GLBA preempts state law only to the extent of an inconsistency.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6807(b)
notes.evidence: is not inconsistent with the provisions of this subchapter if the protection such statute, regulation, order, or interpretation affords any person is greater than the protection provided under this subchapter

notes.front: A state requires banks to get opt-in consent before sharing customer data with non-affiliated third parties. Does the GLBA override it?
notes.back: C: no, a state law giving greater protection is not inconsistent with the GLBA.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the GLBA occupies the field
B) Yes, because the GLBA uses opt-out
C) No, a state law giving greater protection is not inconsistent with the GLBA
D) Only for national banks
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: the GLBA sets a floor and preserves state laws except for inconsistencies. D: the provision has no such bank-type split.
notes.explanation: Opt-in gives consumers more protection than the GLBA opt-out, so it is not treated as inconsistent.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 94 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act privacy provisions), § 6807(a)
notes.evidence: shall not be construed as superseding, altering, or affecting any statute, regulation, order, or interpretation in effect in any State, except to the extent that such statute, regulation, order, or interpretation is inconsistent

notes.front: How does Regulation P treat a university that is also a financial institution, such as for student loans?
notes.back: If it complies with FERPA, it is deemed to comply with Regulation P.
notes.explanation: FERPA compliance substitutes for the Regulation P requirements for such institutions.
notes.source: 12 CFR part 1016 (Regulation P), 2026 edition, § 1016.1(b)(2), p. 2
notes.evidence: shall be deemed to be in compliance with this part if it is in compliance with FERPA

notes.front: If an institution uses a service provider as its qualified individual, what must it keep?
notes.back: Responsibility for complying with the Safeguards Rule, and a senior member of its own staff to direct and oversee the provider.
notes.explanation: Outsourcing the role does not outsource the duty.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(a)(1)–(2), p. 7
notes.evidence: To the extent the requirement in this paragraph (a) is met using a service provider or an affiliate, you shall: (1) Retain responsibility for compliance with this part

notes.front: How often must the qualified individual report in writing to the board of directors?
notes.back: Regularly and at least annually.
notes.explanation: Without a board, the report goes to a senior officer responsible for the programme.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(i), p. 9
notes.evidence: Require your Qualified Individual to report in writing, regularly and at least annually, to your board of directors or equivalent governing body.

notes.front: A small mortgage broker hires an outside security firm to act as its qualified individual. The broker says security is now "the firm's problem". Is that right?
notes.back: A: no, the broker keeps responsibility for compliance and must name a senior staff member to oversee the firm.
notes.choices:
A) No, the broker keeps responsibility for compliance and must name a senior staff member to oversee the firm
B) Yes, outsourcing transfers all duties
C) Yes, if the contract says so
D) No, a qualified individual must always be an employee
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: the Rule says the institution retains responsibility. D: the Rule allows an affiliate or service provider to fill the role.
notes.explanation: The Rule allows an outside qualified individual but keeps compliance responsibility with the institution.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(a), p. 7
notes.evidence: The Qualified Individual may be employed by you, an affiliate, or a service provider.

notes.front: What must the Safeguards Rule information security programme be based on?
notes.back: A risk assessment identifying reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information.
notes.explanation: The risks considered are those to security, confidentiality and integrity.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(b), p. 7
notes.evidence: Base your information security program on a risk assessment that identifies reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information

notes.front: Under the Safeguards Rule, when must customer information be encrypted?
notes.back: Both in transit over external networks and at rest.
notes.explanation: Where encryption is infeasible, the qualified individual may approve effective alternative controls.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(c)(3), p. 7
notes.evidence: Protect by encryption all customer information held or transmitted by you both in transit over external networks and at rest.

notes.front: Who must use multi-factor authentication under the Safeguards Rule?
notes.back: Any individual accessing any information system, unless the qualified individual approves equivalent or stronger controls in writing.
notes.explanation: The exception needs written approval.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(c)(5), p. 8
notes.evidence: Implement multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any information system, unless your Qualified Individual has approved in writing the use of reasonably equivalent or more secure access controls

notes.front: Without continuous monitoring, how often must a Safeguards Rule institution run penetration tests and vulnerability assessments?
notes.back: Penetration testing annually; vulnerability assessments at least every six months.
notes.explanation: Extra assessments are also needed after material changes to operations.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(d)(2), p. 8
notes.evidence: Annual penetration testing of your information systems determined each given year based on relevant identified risks in accordance with the risk assessment

notes.front: Which plan must a Safeguards Rule institution establish for security events?
notes.back: A written incident response plan to promptly respond to and recover from events materially affecting customer information.
notes.explanation: The plan covers events affecting confidentiality, integrity or availability.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(h), p. 9
notes.evidence: Establish a written incident response plan designed to promptly respond to, and recover from, any security event materially affecting the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of customer information in your control.

notes.front: Which Safeguards Rule duties do not apply to institutions holding information on fewer than 5,000 consumers?
notes.back: The written risk assessment, penetration and vulnerability testing, the written incident response plan, and the annual board report.
notes.explanation: The exception is written by paragraph numbers: 314.4(b)(1), (d)(2), (h) and (i).
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.6, p. 10
notes.evidence: Section 314.4(b)(1), (d)(2), (h), and (i) do not apply to financial institutions that maintain customer information concerning fewer than five thousand consumers.

notes.front: A car dealership that arranges financing lets staff log into its customer-finance system with a password only. Nobody has approved an alternative. Which Safeguards Rule duty is unmet?
notes.back: B: multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing the system.
notes.choices:
A) The annual board report
B) Multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing the system
C) Notification to the FTC
D) The written incident response plan
notes.choicesExplained: A and D: nothing suggests these are missing. C: FTC notice follows a notification event, not a design weakness.
notes.explanation: The Rule requires multi-factor authentication unless the qualified individual approves equivalent controls in writing.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(c)(5), p. 8
notes.evidence: Implement multi-factor authentication for any individual accessing any information system

notes.front: What is a notification event under the Safeguards Rule?
notes.back: Acquisition of unencrypted customer information without the authorisation of the person it concerns.
notes.explanation: Information counts as unencrypted if the encryption key was accessed by an unauthorised person.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.2(m), p. 5
notes.evidence: Notification event means acquisition of unencrypted customer information without the authorization of the individual to which the information pertains.

notes.front: A notification event involving at least {{c1::500}} consumers must be reported to the FTC no later than 30 days after discovery.
notes.explanation: The notice is made electronically on a form on the FTC website.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(j)(1), p. 9
notes.evidence: if the notification event involves the information of at least 500 consumers, you must notify the Federal Trade Commission as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery of the event

notes.front: A tax preparer discovers that a thief copied unencrypted files on 800 clients. What does the Safeguards Rule require?
notes.back: C: notify the FTC as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery.
notes.choices:
A) Notify the FTC within 60 calendar days
B) Nothing, as fewer than 1,000 consumers are affected
C) Notify the FTC as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery
D) Notify HHS within 60 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: 60 days is a HIPAA and Health Breach Notification Rule period, not this one. B: the threshold is 500. D: HHS handles HIPAA breaches.
notes.explanation: An acquisition of unencrypted information of 500 or more consumers triggers FTC notice within 30 days.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 314 (Safeguards Rule), 2026 edition, § 314.4(j)(1), p. 9
notes.evidence: you must notify the Federal Trade Commission as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery of the event

notes.front: What is a "red flag" under the Red Flags Rule?
notes.back: A pattern, practice or specific activity that indicates the possible existence of identity theft.
notes.explanation: The Program is built around identifying and responding to these signals.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(b)(9), p. 1
notes.evidence: Red Flag means a pattern, practice, or specific activity that indicates the possible existence of identity theft.

notes.front: Which Identity Theft Prevention Program element picks the warning signs relevant to the institution's accounts?
notes.back: Identifying relevant red flags for its covered accounts and incorporating them into the Program.
notes.explanation: It is the first of four required elements.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(2)(i), p. 2
notes.evidence: Identify relevant Red Flags for the covered accounts that the financial institution or creditor offers or maintains, and incorporate those Red Flags into its Program

notes.front: Which Program element is about spotting warning signs as they happen?
notes.back: Detecting the red flags that have been incorporated into the Program.
notes.explanation: It is the second required element.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(2)(ii), p. 2
notes.evidence: Detect Red Flags that have been incorporated into the Program of the financial institution or creditor

notes.front: Which Program element deals with what staff do once a warning sign is found?
notes.back: Responding appropriately to detected red flags to prevent and mitigate identity theft.
notes.explanation: It is the third required element.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(2)(iii), p. 2
notes.evidence: Respond appropriately to any Red Flags that are detected pursuant to paragraph (d)(2)(ii) of this section to prevent and mitigate identity theft

notes.front: Which Program element keeps it current as threats change?
notes.back: Updating the Program, including its red flags, periodically to reflect changing risks.
notes.explanation: It is the fourth required element.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(2)(iv), p. 2
notes.evidence: Ensure the Program (including the Red Flags determined to be relevant) is updated periodically, to reflect changes in risks to customers

notes.front: A mobile phone company flags new-account applications where the identity-document photo does not match the applicant, then calls the applicant back before activation. Which Program elements does this show?
notes.back: D: detecting a red flag and responding to it.
notes.choices:
A) Board approval only
B) Updating the Program
C) Identifying covered accounts
D) Detecting a red flag and responding to it
notes.choicesExplained: A: board approval is administration, not an element here. B: nothing is being updated. C: identifying accounts is a prior step.
notes.explanation: Spotting the mismatch is detection; the call-back is the response to prevent identity theft.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(d)(2)(ii)–(iii), p. 2
notes.evidence: Detect Red Flags that have been incorporated into the Program of the financial institution or creditor; (iii) Respond appropriately to any Red Flags that are detected

notes.front: Which of these is given in the Red Flags Rule as an example of a covered account?
notes.back: B: a utility account.
notes.choices:
A) A one-off cash purchase
B) A utility account
C) A newspaper subscription paid in advance
D) A company's supplier invoice
notes.choicesExplained: A: a single transaction does not involve multiple payments. C and D: these are not among the examples, and D is not a consumer account.
notes.explanation: The Rule lists utility, mobile phone, credit card, loan and bank accounts as examples.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 681 (Red Flags Rule), 2026 edition, § 681.1(b)(3)(i), p. 1
notes.evidence: margin account, cell phone account, utility account, checking account, or savings account

notes.front: A payday lender hides a large fee in fine print that borrowers cannot reasonably understand. Which federal body can act against it for an abusive practice?
notes.back: A: the CFPB.
notes.choices:
A) The CFPB
B) The Department of Education
C) Only a state court
D) No one, as fees are a private matter
notes.choicesExplained: B: education is unrelated. C: federal UDAAP powers belong to the Bureau. D: the Bureau may act to prevent abusive practices.
notes.explanation: The Bureau may act to prevent covered persons from engaging in unfair, deceptive or abusive practices.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(a)
notes.evidence: The Bureau may take any action authorized under part E to prevent a covered person or service provider from committing or engaging in an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice

notes.front: What are the two main ways an act or practice can be "abusive" under the UDAAP provision?
notes.back: It materially interferes with understanding a term or condition; or it takes unreasonable advantage of the consumer.
notes.explanation: Unreasonable advantage covers a lack of understanding, inability to protect oneself, or reasonable reliance on the provider.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(d)
notes.evidence: materially interferes with the ability of a consumer to understand a term or condition of a consumer financial product or service; or (2) takes unreasonable advantage of

notes.front: What must the CFPB reasonably conclude before declaring a practice unfair?
notes.back: That it causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that they cannot reasonably avoid and is not outweighed by benefits.
notes.explanation: The Bureau must have a reasonable basis for that conclusion before it can declare the practice unlawful as unfair.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(c)(1)
notes.evidence: the act or practice causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers which is not reasonably avoidable by consumers; and (B) such substantial injury is not outweighed by countervailing benefits

notes.front: A lender tells borrowers it will act in their best interests, then steers them into costly products it profits from. Which UDAAP category fits best?
notes.back: C: abusive, as it takes unreasonable advantage of reasonable reliance on the lender.
notes.choices:
A) Unfair only
B) None: marketing is exempt
C) Abusive, as it takes unreasonable advantage of reasonable reliance on the lender
D) A GLBA pretexting offence
notes.choicesExplained: A: unfairness needs substantial unavoidable injury; the reliance element points to abuse. B: there is no marketing exemption. D: pretexting concerns obtaining customer information by false pretences.
notes.explanation: Taking unreasonable advantage of reasonable reliance on a covered person to act in the consumer's interests is abusive.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(d)(2)(C)
notes.evidence: the reasonable reliance by the consumer on a covered person to act in the interests of the consumer

notes.front: How does the CFPB's UDAAP power differ from the FTC's power over unfair or deceptive acts or practices?
notes.back: UDAAP adds "abusive" practices and is limited to consumer financial products or services.
notes.explanation: Both share unfairness and deception; the abusive category is the CFPB addition.
notes.source: 12 U.S.C. § 5531 (unfair, deceptive or abusive acts or practices), § 5531(a)
notes.evidence: an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice under Federal law in connection with any transaction with a consumer for a consumer financial product or service
uses: unfair or deceptive acts or practices

notes.front: Which schools and agencies must follow FERPA?
notes.back: Educational agencies and institutions that receive funds under any program administered by the Secretary of Education.
notes.explanation: The statute withholds funds from institutions that deny parents their rights.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.1(a), p. 2
notes.evidence: this part applies to an educational agency or institution to which funds have been made available under any program administered by the Secretary
uses: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act

notes.front: A private tutoring centre receives no Department of Education funds. Does FERPA govern its student files?
notes.back: D: no, FERPA applies to institutions receiving funds under programmes the Secretary administers.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, FERPA covers all schools
B) Yes, if it teaches minors
C) Only if it has over 100 students
D) No, FERPA applies to institutions receiving funds under programmes the Secretary administers
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: coverage depends on receiving such funds, not on type, age or size.
notes.explanation: FERPA's reach is tied to federal education funding.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.1(a), p. 2
notes.evidence: applies to an educational agency or institution to which funds have been made available under any program administered by the Secretary
uses: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act

notes.front: Are a teacher's private notes, kept only as a memory aid and shown to no one, education records?
notes.back: No, if kept in the sole possession of the maker and shared only with a temporary substitute.
notes.explanation: This is the first exclusion from the definition.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Education records" (b)(1), p. 4
notes.evidence: Records that are kept in the sole possession of the maker, are used only as a personal memory aid, and are not accessible or revealed to any other person except a temporary substitute for the maker of the record.

notes.front: Are records of a school's law enforcement unit education records?
notes.back: No, they are excluded, subject to § 99.8.
notes.explanation: This is the second exclusion from the definition.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Education records" (b)(2), p. 4
notes.evidence: Records of the law enforcement unit of an educational agency or institution, subject to the provisions of § 99.8.

notes.front: Which medical records of an eligible student are excluded from education records?
notes.back: Records made by a physician or other professional, used only for treating the student and shared only with those providing treatment.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must be met for the exclusion.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Education records" (b)(4), p. 4
notes.evidence: Made, maintained, or used only in connection with treatment of the student; and (iii) Disclosed only to individuals providing the treatment.

notes.front: A college keeps a student's disciplinary file in the dean's office, available to staff who handle conduct cases. Is it an education record?
notes.back: A: yes, it is directly related to the student and maintained by the institution.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is directly related to the student and maintained by the institution
B) No, disciplinary files are law enforcement records
C) No, it is a sole-possession record
D) No, only grades are education records
notes.choicesExplained: B: the dean's office is not a law enforcement unit. C: other staff can see it. D: the definition is not limited to grades.
notes.explanation: Records directly related to a student and kept by the institution are education records unless an exclusion applies.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Education records" (a), p. 4
notes.evidence: (1) Directly related to a student; and (2) Maintained by an educational agency or institution

notes.front: What happens to FERPA rights when a student becomes an eligible student?
notes.back: The rights and consent powers held by the parents transfer to the student.
notes.explanation: Schools may still disclose to parents in some cases listed in § 99.31, such as a health or safety emergency.
notes.source: 20 U.S.C. § 1232g (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act), § 1232g(d)
notes.evidence: the permission or consent required of and the rights accorded to the parents of the student shall thereafter only be required of and accorded to the student
uses: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act

notes.front: A 17-year-old attends a state university. Her father asks the university to show him her transcript. Whose FERPA rights apply?
notes.back: B: hers, as she attends a postsecondary institution.
notes.choices:
A) Her father's, until she turns 18
B) Hers, as she attends a postsecondary institution
C) Both equally
D) Neither, as universities are exempt
notes.choicesExplained: A: attending postsecondary education is enough on its own. C: the rights transfer. D: funded universities are covered.
notes.explanation: Rights transfer when a student turns 18 or attends a postsecondary institution.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Eligible student", p. 5
notes.evidence: a student who has reached 18 years of age or is attending an institution of postsecondary education

notes.front: A school must comply with a request to inspect education records within a reasonable time, but not more than {{c1::45}} days.
notes.explanation: The school must also answer reasonable requests for explanations of the records.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.10(b), p. 7
notes.evidence: shall comply with a request for access to records within a reasonable period of time, but not more than 45 days after it has received the request

notes.front: A parent of a 10-year-old asks to see his son's school file on 1 March. What is the latest the school can comply?
notes.back: C: 45 days after receiving the request.
notes.choices:
A) 30 days after the request
B) 60 days after the request
C) 45 days after receiving the request
D) At the end of the school year
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: FERPA's cap is 45 days. D: FERPA sets a day limit, not a term-based one.
notes.explanation: FERPA allows a reasonable period, capped at 45 days.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.10(b), p. 7
notes.evidence: but not more than 45 days after it has received the request

notes.front: If a school refuses to amend a record a parent says is inaccurate, what can the parent ask for?
notes.back: A hearing to challenge the record.
notes.explanation: If the hearing goes against them, they may place a statement in the record explaining their disagreement.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.21(a), p. 9
notes.evidence: an opportunity for a hearing to challenge the content of the student's education records on the grounds that the information contained in the education records is inaccurate, misleading

notes.front: What must FERPA written consent to disclosure specify?
notes.back: The records that may be disclosed, the purpose of the disclosure, and the party or class of parties receiving them.
notes.explanation: The consent must also be signed and dated.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.30(b), p. 10
notes.evidence: The written consent must: (1) Specify the records that may be disclosed; (2) State the purpose of the disclosure; and (3) Identify the party or class of parties to whom the disclosure may be made.

notes.front: A school wants to give a scholarship foundation a pupil's grades. No exception applies. What does it need?
notes.back: D: signed, dated written consent naming the records, the purpose and the foundation.
notes.choices:
A) Oral permission from the pupil
B) Nothing, grades are directory information
C) A notice in the school newsletter
D) Signed, dated written consent naming the records, the purpose and the foundation
notes.choicesExplained: A: consent must be written, signed and dated. B: grades are not in the directory information list. C: notice is not consent.
notes.explanation: Without an exception, disclosure requires written consent meeting § 99.30.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.30(a), p. 10
notes.evidence: The parent or eligible student shall provide a signed and dated written consent before an educational agency or institution discloses personally identifiable information

notes.front: To which school officials may records be disclosed without consent?
notes.back: Officials, including teachers, whom the school has determined have legitimate educational interests.
notes.explanation: Contractors can count as school officials under conditions.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(1)(i)(A), p. 10
notes.evidence: The disclosure is to other school officials, including teachers, within the agency or institution whom the agency or institution has determined to have legitimate educational interests.

notes.front: When can an outside contractor, such as a cloud learning platform, be treated as a school official?
notes.back: When it performs a function staff would otherwise do, is under the school's direct control over the records, and follows FERPA's redisclosure limits.
notes.explanation: All the listed conditions apply together.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B), p. 10
notes.evidence: Performs an institutional service or function for which the agency or institution would otherwise use employees; (2) Is under the direct control of the agency or institution with respect to the use and maintenance of education records

notes.front: May a school send a pupil's records without consent to a school where the pupil intends to enrol?
notes.back: Yes, subject to the conditions in § 99.34.
notes.explanation: The exception also covers a school where the student is already enrolled.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(2), p. 10
notes.evidence: to officials of another school, school system, or institution of postsecondary education where the student seeks or intends to enroll

notes.front: Before complying with a subpoena for education records, what must a school usually do?
notes.back: Make a reasonable effort to notify the parent or eligible student in advance.
notes.explanation: The advance notice lets them seek protective action.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(9)(ii), p. 12
notes.evidence: only if the agency or institution makes a reasonable effort to notify the parent or eligible student of the order or subpoena in advance of compliance

notes.front: Which FERPA exception allows disclosure when a student threatens others?
notes.back: Disclosure in connection with a health or safety emergency, under § 99.36.
notes.explanation: The school must record the threat that formed the basis for the disclosure and who received it.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(10), p. 12
notes.evidence: The disclosure is in connection with a health or safety emergency, under the conditions described in § 99.36.

notes.front: A school's contracted online homework platform needs pupils' names and grades to run. The school controls how the data is used. Does the school need parental consent to share it?
notes.back: B: no, the provider can be treated as a school official with legitimate educational interests.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, every outside party needs consent
B) No, the provider can be treated as a school official with legitimate educational interests
C) No, because grades are directory information
D) Yes, unless the pupils are over 13
notes.choicesExplained: A: contractors meeting the conditions count as school officials. C: grades are not directory information. D: age 13 is a COPPA threshold, not FERPA's.
notes.explanation: An outsourced function under the school's direct control can fall within the school official exception.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.31(a)(1)(i)(B), p. 10
notes.evidence: A contractor, consultant, volunteer, or other party to whom an agency or institution has outsourced institutional services or functions may be considered a school official

notes.front: What are three items FERPA lists as directory information?
notes.back: Any three of: name, address, telephone listing, email, photograph, date of birth, major, dates of attendance, degrees and awards.
notes.explanation: The list says directory information includes, but is not limited to, these items.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Directory information" (a), p. 3
notes.evidence: Directory information includes, but is not limited to, the student's name; address; telephone listing; electronic mail address; photograph; date and place of birth; major field of study

notes.front: Which identifier can never be directory information?
notes.back: A student's social security number.
notes.explanation: A student identification number is also excluded unless it cannot be used alone to access records.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.3, "Directory information" (b), p. 3
notes.evidence: Directory information does not include a student's- (1) Social security number

notes.front: Before disclosing directory information, what must a school give public notice of?
notes.back: The types designated as directory information, the right to refuse designation, and the deadline to object in writing.
notes.explanation: Parents and eligible students in attendance receive this notice.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.37(a), p. 17
notes.evidence: A parent's or eligible student's right to refuse to let the agency or institution designate any or all of those types of information about the student as directory information

notes.front: A high school gave public notice of its directory information list. One parent objected in writing on time. The school later publishes all pupils' names in a sports programme. What is the problem?
notes.back: A: the objecting parent's child should have been left out.
notes.choices:
A) The objecting parent's child should have been left out
B) None: directory information is always public
C) The school needed every parent's written consent
D) Sports programmes can never name pupils
notes.choicesExplained: B: parents have the right to refuse designation. C: consent is not required for properly noticed directory information. D: names are standard directory information.
notes.explanation: A parent may refuse to let the school designate information about their child as directory information.
notes.source: 34 CFR part 99 (FERPA regulations), 2025 edition, § 99.37(a)(2), p. 17
notes.evidence: A parent's or eligible student's right to refuse to let the agency or institution designate any or all of those types of information about the student as directory information

notes.front: A school nurse keeps immunisation records in a public school's student files. Are they HIPAA protected health information or FERPA education records?
notes.back: FERPA education records: HIPAA excludes information in education records covered by FERPA.
notes.explanation: The HIPAA definition of protected health information carves out FERPA education records.
notes.source: 45 CFR part 160 (HIPAA general administrative requirements), 2025 edition, § 160.103, "Protected health information" (2)(i), p. 7
notes.evidence: In education records covered by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, as amended, 20 U.S.C. 1232g

notes.front: What are three topics a student cannot be required to reveal in a funded survey without consent under the PPRA?
notes.back: Any three of: political beliefs; mental problems; sex behaviour; illegal conduct; family appraisals; privileged relationships; religion; income.
notes.explanation: The statute lists eight protected categories.
notes.source: 20 U.S.C. § 1232h (protection of pupil rights), § 1232h(b)
notes.evidence: political affiliations or beliefs of the student or the student's parent; (2) mental or psychological problems of the student or the student's family; (3) sex behavior or attitudes

notes.front: Under the PPRA, whose consent is needed before an unemancipated minor takes a survey on protected topics?
notes.back: The parent's prior written consent.
notes.explanation: An adult or emancipated student gives their own prior consent.
notes.source: 20 U.S.C. § 1232h (protection of pupil rights), § 1232h(b)
notes.evidence: in the case of an unemancipated minor, without the prior written consent of the parent

notes.front: A federally funded middle-school programme requires pupils to complete a survey asking about their parents' religious practices. What does the PPRA require?
notes.back: C: the parents' prior written consent.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, surveys are always allowed
B) Only the pupils' agreement
C) The parents' prior written consent
D) Approval from the FTC
notes.choicesExplained: A: religious practices are a protected category. B: unemancipated minors need parental consent. D: the FTC has no role here.
notes.explanation: Religious practices of the student or parent are protected; minors need prior written parental consent.
notes.source: 20 U.S.C. § 1232h (protection of pupil rights), § 1232h(b)(7)
notes.evidence: religious practices, affiliations, or beliefs of the student or student's parent
